sections.text: Buying beats renting only after you have owned long enough to recover the transaction costs, and that point depends heavily on the assumptions. In the example below, a $380,000 home against $2,300 monthly rent breaks even in year 9 in the Rent vs. Buy Calculator, not in year 3 or 4. Move the home's annual appreciation from 3% to 0% and it becomes year 22; move it to 5% and it becomes year 4. The break-even year is a result of your inputs, so the useful skill is knowing which inputs matter.

For each year, the calculator adds up the net cost of each path. For buying: the down payment and closing costs, mortgage principal and interest, property tax, maintenance and mortgage insurance while the loan is above 80% of the price, minus the cash you would get from selling after selling costs and repaying the loan. For renting: all rent (rising each year) plus renters insurance, minus the growth the down payment and closing costs would have earned if invested instead. The break-even year is the first year buying has the lower net cost.

items: Home price $380,000, 10% down ($38,000), 30-year fixed at 6.5%. Loan $342,000, payment of principal and interest $2,162.

Closing costs 3% ($11,400), selling costs 6%, property tax 1.2% of the price a year, maintenance 1.5% of the home value a year, mortgage insurance 0.7% of the loan a year until the balance reaches 80% of the price, home appreciation 3% a year.
Rent $2,300 a month, rising 3% a year, plus $180 a year for renters insurance.

The renter invests the down payment and closing costs at an assumed 7% a year. That figure is built into the calculator and is an assumption, not a promise. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
Taxes on investment gains, mortgage interest deductions and the sale gain are left out.

sections.text: A positive difference means buying has cost more so far. The gap closes slowly because the early years carry $11,400 of closing costs, mortgage insurance, and a sale cost of 6% that you would pay if you left. After year 8, rent keeps rising while the mortgage payment does not, and the gap flips.
Which input changes the answer the most

Three inputs dominate: how fast the home gains value, how high rent is compared with the monthly cost of owning, and the mortgage rate. Appreciation is the least certain and the most powerful, so test it at 0% as well as your best guess. The down payment barely matters here, partly because a bigger one saves interest but gives up more investment growth.

The model charges the buyer the extra monthly cost of owning but does not credit the renter for investing that monthly difference. In the first year, owning costs about $11,000 more in cash than renting in this example, so the renter could be investing that cash, which would push the true break-even later. Other simplifications cut both ways: it assumes steady 3% appreciation and a steady 7% investment return, and it omits tax effects on both sides. Treat the year as an estimate with a wide margin.

items: Comparing the mortgage payment with rent. Property tax, insurance, maintenance and mortgage insurance often add a large share on top of principal and interest.
Assuming prices always rise. Test a flat-price case.
Ignoring selling costs. At a 6% assumption, selling a home worth $380,000 costs $22,800, and more as the home appreciates: $26,431 at the value it reaches in year 5.
Treating "rent is wasted money" as a fact. Rent buys housing; interest, taxes and maintenance are also costs that never come back.
Leaving out the intangible side: renting offers flexibility, owning offers stability. The numbers cannot value either.

sections.text: When this analysis does not apply

If you may move within a few years, buying is rarely cheaper unless prices rise fast. If rent is far below ownership costs where you live, the break-even can be decades away or never come. If you plan to stay for life and can afford the payment, the comparison becomes a question of budget and lifestyle. Enter your own price, rent, rate and expected stay into the Rent vs. Buy Calculator, and read the year-by-year chart, not just the headline year.
